Step 0 · The Number Line Is Not Enough

The Number Line Is Not Enough: Where Does the Solution of x² = −1 Stand?

This step answers one question: the solution of x² = −1 — where does it stand? You already know: the real numbers fill a single line, and every real square is ≥ 0 — positive squared is positive, negative squared is positive, 0 squared is 0. The probe below lets you check by hand: drag x along the line and the trace above draws every value x² can take; it hugs the region above the line yet never reaches the −1 line. It is not hiding — there is simply no room for it on this line.

Square probe x (drag along the line) x = 1
Stand the line up as one edge: unfold the plane ⤢

Probe x = 1: x² = 1 ≥ 0. Drag x from negative to positive and the square traces a parabola whose lowest point is 0 — a whole unreachable gap away from −1.

Conclusion: x² = −1 has no real solution — what is missing is not a number but a dimension. Add a perpendicular axis to the line and numbers graduate from “points on a line” to “points on a plane”; the unit on the new axis is written i. For now just one promise: on this page i² = −1 becomes something you can see, not something you memorise.

Why a whole new axis, and not just one extra point? Because numbers must stay computable: the new point added to, and multiplied by, the old reals must have somewhere to land — only a whole plane holds the entire new number system. Next stop: learn to read “a point on the plane” fluently.

Start exploring ↓

text:
← Knowledge Index

Complex Numbers · Multiplication Is Rotation Plus Scaling

In the textbook, i drops out of the sky: “define i² = −1”. You memorise it, you can compute with it, but you never learn what it is. This page tells it differently: first bring numbers back from a line onto a plane — a complex number (a number of the form a + bi, with a and b real) is a point on the plane, an arrow; addition slides the arrow, multiplication rotates and scales it. Then i² = −1 needs no memorising: multiplying by i is a 90° turn, and two turns point you exactly at −1. Every modulus, argument, sum and product on this page is computed on the spot from (a, b) alone — picture and readout share one source.

Step 1 · A Point on the Complex Plane

A Complex Number Is a Point: Pin It by (a, b), or by (Modulus, Argument)

This step answers: how many numbers does it take to pin down one complex number? The picture is a complex plane: horizontal real axis, vertical imaginary axis. Drag the point z and all four readouts are computed live from its coordinates (a, b): a is the real part, b is the imaginary part (mind this: the imaginary part is the real number b itself, without the i), written z = a + bi; the arrow from the origin to z has length called the modulus |z| — the hypotenuse of Pythagoras’ theorem; the angle from the positive real axis, measured counter-clockwise, is the argument θ. Arguments have many equivalent writings; this page always uses the principal value: the one normalised into (−180°, 180°].

Coordinate entry · keyboard or numbers

Enter finite coordinates. Tab moves between controls; ↑/↓ changes only the draft by0.1. Enter or Apply updates the plot. As with dragging, coordinates snap to a0.1 grid before the drawing limit below is applied. The readouts show the actual applied values.

Drawing range: each component is clipped to−5…5. This limits the drawing, not complex numbers themselves.

z · Real part Re
z · Imaginary part Im (without i)
Apply coordinates

Preset tour:
3 + 4i
−4 (pure real)
3i (pure imaginary)
On the unit circle · 50°

z ≈ 3 + 4i: real part a ≈ 3, imaginary part b ≈ 4; modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 5 (computed by Pythagoras); argument θ ≈ 53.1° (counter-clockwise from the positive real axis). Displayed numbers are rounded after calculation from unrounded coordinates.

Conclusion: there are two ways to pin the point — coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument). They are two readings of the same arrow: one says “how far right, how far up”, the other says “how long, pointing which way”. Addition next door reads most naturally in the first; multiplication will need the second — get fluent in both.

Check the boundaries one by one: drag the point onto the negative real axis and the argument reads +180°, not −180° — the right end of the principal interval is closed. On the unit circle (the dashed ring) the modulus stays 1 and only the angle moves; there the arrow tip’s coordinates are exactly (cos θ, sin θ) — that reading is established in Step 1 of the trigonometry page.

Step 2 · Addition

Addition = Sliding: the Sum’s Coordinates Are the Two Sides Added Separately

This step answers: when two complex numbers are added, what actually moves in the picture? Two draggable arrows z₁ and z₂ are on stage; the green arrow is their sum z₁ + z₂, drawn by the parallelogram rule (span a parallelogram with z₁, z₂ as adjacent sides and the diagonal is the sum; equivalently, attach z₂’s arrow head-to-tail at z₁’s tip — same landing point). Drag either arrow and the three check rows below verify, row by row, that the sum’s real and imaginary parts are exactly the two sides added separately.

Coordinate entry · keyboard or numbers

Enter finite coordinates. Tab moves between controls; ↑/↓ changes only the draft by0.1. Enter or Apply updates the plot. As with dragging, coordinates snap to a0.1 grid before the drawing limit below is applied. The readouts show the actual applied values.

Drawing range: each input component is clipped to−4.2…4.2; their sum is still calculated from the two numbers. This is a drawing limit only.

Complex number to edit

z₁ · first number
z₂ · second number
z₁ · Real part Re
z₁ · Imaginary part Im (without i)
Apply coordinates

z₁ = 2 + i, z₂ = 1 + 2i, z₁ + z₂ = 3 + 3i

Real-part check: 2 + 1 = 3 ✓ (exactly the sum’s real part)

Imaginary-part check: 1 + 2 = 3 ✓ (exactly the sum’s imaginary part)

Conclusion: adding z₂ slides the whole picture along z₂’s arrow by exactly that much; the sum’s horizontal and vertical coordinates are the two sides added separately. It is the same thing as vector addition — complex addition = component-wise addition = translation, and it holds for addition only.

Plant a contrast: multiplication is not component-wise. If (1 + i) × (1 + i) were multiplied component-wise you would get something odd like 1 + 1i; the true answer appears on the bench in Step 4 — multiplication moves modulus and angle, not components.

Step 3 · Multiply by i

Multiply by i: Nothing Changes Except a 90° Turn

This step answers: what is i, itself? Pick a starting point and keep pressing “× i”: each press turns the arrow 90° counter-clockwise — watch the readout: the modulus does not budge, the argument gains exactly +90° each time (wrapping back by the principal value past 180°). Landing points and arcs stay on stage the whole time; press four times and the arrow faces its original direction again. Below runs the unit-point tour: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1, landings pinned one by one on the axes.

Starting point z:
1 (the unit point)
3 + 2i
× i (turn 90°)
Reset ↺
Multiplied by i 0 times (every 4 turns restore the direction)

Current z = 1: modulus = 1 (identical before and after ×i); argument = 0°.

The unit-point tour (all computed by repeated multiplication): i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Watch where i² lands: two 90° turns from 1 are a 180° about-face, landing on −1.

The verdict: ×i = a 90° counter-clockwise rotation, so i² = two turns = an about-face = −1. i² = −1 is turned into existence, not memorised into it. “i is the notation for √−1” and “i is the action of turning 90°” are two faces of the same i: the first is its name, the second is its behaviour.

Switch the start to 3 + 2i and press four more times: the landings are off-axis, yet the modulus stays √13 throughout, the argument gains 90° each press, and the fourth press lands exactly back on (3, 2) — period 4 holds for every start, because four turns are one full turn.

Step 4 · General Multiplication

General Multiplication = Moduli Multiply, Arguments Add: the Checking Bench

This step answers: multiplying by an arbitrary complex number — what happens to modulus and to angle? First verify the two halves separately: multiplying by a positive real (preset 2 below) only scales and never turns; multiplying by a number of modulus 1 only turns and never scales. An arbitrary multiplier z₂ stacks the two. Drag z₁ (the multiplicand) and z₂ (the multiplier); the green arrow is the product z₁·z₂. The bench below checks three groups, all computed live: the modulus check, the angle check, and an algebraic route (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂) — two roads, one source, cross-verified.

Coordinate entry · keyboard or numbers

Enter finite coordinates. Tab moves between controls; ↑/↓ changes only the draft by0.1. Enter or Apply updates the plot. As with dragging, coordinates snap to a0.1 grid before the drawing limit below is applied. The readouts show the actual applied values.

Drawing range: each input number has modulus at most2.6. After snapping, a point outside the disk is scaled toward the origin to the boundary without changing its angle; the resulting components need not remain on the0.1 grid. This is a drawing limit only.

Try setting both numbers to1+i using coordinates. Predict the product’s modulus and angle, then apply and compare the plot with the readouts.

Complex number to edit

z₁ · first number
z₂ · second number
z₂ · Real part Re
z₂ · Imaginary part Im (without i)
Apply coordinates

Set the multiplier z₂ to a preset:
2 (pure real · scale only)
Modulus 1 · 60° (rotate only)
1 + i (turn 45°, scale by √2)

The symbolic identities are exact. Displayed components and moduli use up to2 decimal places; angles use up to1. Do not treat rounded operands as exact when recomputing.

z₁ ≈ 2 + i, z₂ ≈ 1 + i ⟹ z₁·z₂ ≈ 1 + 3i

Modulus identity: |z₁z₂| = |z₁| × |z₂|. Displayed factor moduli: |z₁| ≈ 2.24, |z₂| ≈ 1.41. Multiplying unrounded values gives |z₁|·|z₂| ≈ 3.16; computing the product’s modulus directly gives |z₁z₂| ≈ 3.16.

Angle check: displayed θ₁ ≈ 26.6°, θ₂ ≈ 45°. Adding unrounded angles and normalising to the principal interval gives ≈ 71.6°; the product’s argument calculated directly is ≈ 71.6°.

Algebraic identity: (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂). Displayed coordinates: a₁ ≈ 2, b₁ ≈ 1, a₂ ≈ 1, b₂ ≈ 1. Calculating from unrounded coordinates gives the product ≈ 1 + 3i; the plot uses that same result.

Conclusion: the multiplication law — moduli multiply, arguments add. Multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Conditions, stated: after adding, angles must be normalised into the principal interval (340° and −20° are the same direction; this page writes −20°); if either factor is 0, the product is the origin and has no argument.

This bench keeps both points inside the disc of modulus ≤ 2.6 so the product stays in frame — the law itself holds for complex numbers of any size. Verify a group with preset 1 + i: with z₁ = 2 + i, the product’s argument should be exactly 45° more than before and its modulus exactly √2 times — the bench ticks both on the spot.

Step 5 · Self-Test

Self-Test: Turn It Right, Checked on the Spot

All three verdicts come from the same live computation as the main text: landings from repeated multiplication, moduli from Pythagoras — no pre-written answer table. Get one right and it locks (dragging points in the main text afterwards will not wash the verdict away); get one wrong and the feedback diagnoses your exact wrong turn, and you may retry.

Question 1 · Multiply by i twice

z = 3 + 2i. Multiply by i twice (that is, z·i²) — where does it land? Turn it in your head first: 90° once, then 90° again.

3 − 2i
−3 − 2i
−3 + 2i
3 + 2i

Question 2 · Whose modulus is bigger

|3 + 4i| versus |−4 + 3i| — which is bigger? Do not rush: both moduli are computed by Pythagoras; compute first, then compare.

3 + 4i is bigger
−4 + 3i is bigger
They are equal

Question 3 · True or false

Judge this claim: “The modulus of a product equals the sum of the two moduli.”

True
False

Step 6 · Finale

Finale: One Plane, Two Operations

Complex numbers are not a rule to memorise — they are the arithmetic that grows naturally once numbers are put back on the plane. Three closing cards:

A complex number is a point on the plane

z = a + bi corresponds one-to-one with a point of the plane and with an arrow from the origin. Pin it two ways: coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument) — the modulus is the arrow’s length, the argument its direction (principal value (−180°, 180°] on this page).

Addition is sliding

The sum’s coordinates are the two sides’ coordinates added separately; in the picture it is one slide along the added number’s arrow — the diagonal of the parallelogram. Addition moves position only.

Multiplication is rotation + scaling

Moduli multiply, arguments add: multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Multiplying by i is the purest case — modulus 1, angle 90°, rotation with no scaling; and i² = −1 is simply “two turns make an about-face”.

One sentence each for two roads ahead: division is the inverse of multiplication — arguments subtract, moduli divide — not expanded on this page. And one planted thread: if this point starts turning on its own, its angle growing uniformly with time, its position is eiθ running on the unit circle — the doorway to Euler’s formula, named here only.

The very point at angle θ, set turning and with its height unrolled, is the sine wave — watch it move on the trigonometry page →

A rotation matrix has no real eigen-direction; its eigenvalues are a pair of complex numbers, drawn as spirals — see complex numbers make their first matrix appearance on the eigenvalues page →

Phase is a starting angle: where each circle starts on the Fourier page is exactly what this page’s argument is for — see it on the Fourier page →

Step 2 · Addition

Addition = Sliding: the Sum’s Coordinates Are the Two Sides Added Separately

This step answers: when two complex numbers are added, what actually moves in the picture? Two draggable arrows z₁ and z₂ are on stage; the green arrow is their sum z₁ + z₂, drawn by the parallelogram rule (span a parallelogram with z₁, z₂ as adjacent sides and the diagonal is the sum; equivalently, attach z₂’s arrow head-to-tail at z₁’s tip — same landing point). Drag either arrow and the three check rows below verify, row by row, that the sum’s real and imaginary parts are exactly the two sides added separately.

z₁ · Real part Re
z₁ · Imaginary part Im (without i)
Apply coordinates

z₁ = 2 + i, z₂ = 1 + 2i, z₁ + z₂ = 3 + 3i

Real-part check: 2 + 1 = 3 ✓ (exactly the sum’s real part)

Imaginary-part check: 1 + 2 = 3 ✓ (exactly the sum’s imaginary part)

Conclusion: adding z₂ slides the whole picture along z₂’s arrow by exactly that much; the sum’s horizontal and vertical coordinates are the two sides added separately. It is the same thing as vector addition — complex addition = component-wise addition = translation, and it holds for addition only.

Plant a contrast: multiplication is not component-wise. If (1 + i) × (1 + i) were multiplied component-wise you would get something odd like 1 + 1i; the true answer appears on the bench in Step 4 — multiplication moves modulus and angle, not components.

Step 3 · Multiply by i

Multiply by i: Nothing Changes Except a 90° Turn

This step answers: what is i, itself? Pick a starting point and keep pressing “× i”: each press turns the arrow 90° counter-clockwise — watch the readout: the modulus does not budge, the argument gains exactly +90° each time (wrapping back by the principal value past 180°). Landing points and arcs stay on stage the whole time; press four times and the arrow faces its original direction again. Below runs the unit-point tour: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1, landings pinned one by one on the axes.

Starting point z:
1 (the unit point)
3 + 2i
× i (turn 90°)
Reset ↺
Multiplied by i 0 times (every 4 turns restore the direction)

Current z = 1: modulus = 1 (identical before and after ×i); argument = 0°.

The unit-point tour (all computed by repeated multiplication): i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Watch where i² lands: two 90° turns from 1 are a 180° about-face, landing on −1.

The verdict: ×i = a 90° counter-clockwise rotation, so i² = two turns = an about-face = −1. i² = −1 is turned into existence, not memorised into it. “i is the notation for √−1” and “i is the action of turning 90°” are two faces of the same i: the first is its name, the second is its behaviour.

Switch the start to 3 + 2i and press four more times: the landings are off-axis, yet the modulus stays √13 throughout, the argument gains 90° each press, and the fourth press lands exactly back on (3, 2) — period 4 holds for every start, because four turns are one full turn.

Step 4 · General Multiplication

General Multiplication = Moduli Multiply, Arguments Add: the Checking Bench

This step answers: multiplying by an arbitrary complex number — what happens to modulus and to angle? First verify the two halves separately: multiplying by a positive real (preset 2 below) only scales and never turns; multiplying by a number of modulus 1 only turns and never scales. An arbitrary multiplier z₂ stacks the two. Drag z₁ (the multiplicand) and z₂ (the multiplier); the green arrow is the product z₁·z₂. The bench below checks three groups, all computed live: the modulus check, the angle check, and an algebraic route (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂) — two roads, one source, cross-verified.

Set the multiplier z₂ to a preset:

Modulus 1 · 60° (rotate only)

The symbolic identities are exact. Displayed components and moduli use up to2 decimal places; angles use up to1. Do not treat rounded operands as exact when recomputing.

z₁ ≈ 2 + i, z₂ ≈ 1 + i ⟹ z₁·z₂ ≈ 1 + 3i

Modulus identity: |z₁z₂| = |z₁| × |z₂|. Displayed factor moduli: |z₁| ≈ 2.24, |z₂| ≈ 1.41. Multiplying unrounded values gives |z₁|·|z₂| ≈ 3.16; computing the product’s modulus directly gives |z₁z₂| ≈ 3.16.

Angle check: displayed θ₁ ≈ 26.6°, θ₂ ≈ 45°. Adding unrounded angles and normalising to the principal interval gives ≈ 71.6°; the product’s argument calculated directly is ≈ 71.6°.

Algebraic identity: (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂). Displayed coordinates: a₁ ≈ 2, b₁ ≈ 1, a₂ ≈ 1, b₂ ≈ 1. Calculating from unrounded coordinates gives the product ≈ 1 + 3i; the plot uses that same result.

Conclusion: the multiplication law — moduli multiply, arguments add. Multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Conditions, stated: after adding, angles must be normalised into the principal interval (340° and −20° are the same direction; this page writes −20°); if either factor is 0, the product is the origin and has no argument.

This bench keeps both points inside the disc of modulus ≤ 2.6 so the product stays in frame — the law itself holds for complex numbers of any size. Verify a group with preset 1 + i: with z₁ = 2 + i, the product’s argument should be exactly 45° more than before and its modulus exactly √2 times — the bench ticks both on the spot.

|3 + 4i| versus |−4 + 3i| — which is bigger? Do not rush: both moduli are computed by Pythagoras; compute first, then compare.

3 + 4i is bigger
−4 + 3i is bigger
They are equal

✓ Correct: |3 + 4i| = 5 and |−4 + 3i| = 5 — equal. The two points point in different directions yet sit at the same distance from the origin: the modulus sees length only, never direction.

Question 3 · True or false

Judge this claim: “The modulus of a product equals the sum of the two moduli.”

False

✗ The claim is actually false. Test it with numbers on the spot: with z₁ = z₂ = 1 + i, the product’s modulus is 2; the product of the moduli is 2 and the sum of the moduli is 2.83 — which one does the product’s modulus equal? Dragging a group on the Step 4 bench proves it yourself, too.

True

✓ Correct judgment — the claim is false: test it on the spot with a ready-made set of numbers — with z₁ = z₂ = 1 + i, |z₁|·|z₂| = 2, exactly |(1 + i)²| = |2i| = 2; the “sum of moduli” would give 2.83, which does not match. The three, wrapped up: (1) multiplying by i twice is an about-face — both coordinates flip sign; (2) the modulus recognises length only: (3, 4) and (−4, 3) are the same Pythagorean pair, swapped and sign-flipped, both of modulus 5; (3) moduli multiply, arguments add — the “sum” lives on the angle side only; on the modulus side it is always a product.

Step 6 · Finale

Finale: One Plane, Two Operations

Complex numbers are not a rule to memorise — they are the arithmetic that grows naturally once numbers are put back on the plane. Three closing cards:

A complex number is a point on the plane

z = a + bi corresponds one-to-one with a point of the plane and with an arrow from the origin. Pin it two ways: coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument) — the modulus is the arrow’s length, the argument its direction (principal value (−180°, 180°] on this page).

Addition is sliding

The sum’s coordinates are the two sides’ coordinates added separately; in the picture it is one slide along the added number’s arrow — the diagonal of the parallelogram. Addition moves position only.

Multiplication is rotation + scaling

Moduli multiply, arguments add: multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Multiplying by i is the purest case — modulus 1, angle 90°, rotation with no scaling; and i² = −1 is simply “two turns make an about-face”.

One sentence each for two roads ahead: division is the inverse of multiplication — arguments subtract, moduli divide — not expanded on this page. And one planted thread: if this point starts turning on its own, its angle growing uniformly with time, its position is eiθ running on the unit circle — the doorway to Euler’s formula, named here only.

The very point at angle θ, set turning and with its height unrolled, is the sine wave — watch it move on the trigonometry page →

A rotation matrix has no real eigen-direction; its eigenvalues are a pair of complex numbers, drawn as spirals — see complex numbers make their first matrix appearance on the eigenvalues page →

Phase is a starting angle: where each circle starts on the Fourier page is exactly what this page’s argument is for — see it on the Fourier page →

← 知识索引

复数 · 乘法是旋转加伸缩

课本里 i 是空降的：「规定 i² = −1」，背下来、会算、但不知道它是什么。这一页换个讲法：先把数从一条线请回一张平面——复数（形如 a + bi 的数，a、b 都是实数）就是平面上的一个点、一根箭头；加法是把箭头平移，乘法是把箭头旋转加伸缩。于是 i² = −1 不必背：乘 i 就是转 90°，转两次正好掉头指向 −1。这一页所有的模、辐角、和、积，都只由 (a, b) 当场实算，图和读数同源。

中
EN
0 数轴不够用
1 点与箭头
2 加法是平移
3 乘 i 转 90°
4 乘法对账台
5 自测
6 终章

第 0 步 · 数轴不够用

数轴不够用：x² = −1 的解站在哪里？

这一步要回答：方程 x² = −1 的解，到底站在哪里？你已经知道：实数全排在一条数轴上，而任何实数的平方都 ≥ 0——正数平方是正数，负数平方也是正数，0 的平方是 0。下面这台探针让你亲手验：拖着 x 沿数轴走，上方描出的轨迹是 x² 的全部取值，它贴着数轴上方走，却永远够不到 −1 那条横线。找不到不是因为没找仔细——是这条线上根本没有它的位置。

平方探针 x（沿数轴拖） x = −1.5
收起平面 ↩

平面展开了：横着的还是原来那条实轴，新竖起来的这条叫虚轴，两条轴张成的平面叫复平面。原点正上方一个单位的那个点，就是待认领的候选：本页接下来把它认作 i，并一步步验明——它的平方真的是 −1（第 3 步见分晓）。

结论：x² = −1 在实数里无解，缺的不是某个数、是一个维度。给数轴加一条垂直的轴，数就从「线上的点」升级为「平面上的点」；新轴上的单位记作 i。这一步先只承诺一件事：i² = −1 在本页会变成看得见的事实，不靠背。

为什么非得加一整条轴，而不是只添一个点？因为数要能运算：添进来的点和原来的实数相加、相乘，结果还得有地方站——一张平面才装得下这一整套新数。下一站先把「平面上的点」这套读法认全。

开始探索 ↓

第 1 步 · 复平面上的点

复数是平面上的点：钉住它要么 (a, b)，要么（模，辐角）

这一步要回答：一个复数，要几个数才能钉住？图上是一个复平面：横轴是实轴、纵轴是虚轴。拖动点 z，读数四栏全部由它的坐标 (a, b) 当场实算：a 叫实部、b 叫虚部（注意：虚部是 b 这个实数本身，不带 i），写法记作 z = a + bi；从原点向 z 拉出的箭头，长度叫模 |z|——就是勾股定理里那根斜边；箭头与实轴正半轴的夹角（逆时针量）叫辐角 θ。辐角有很多个等价写法，本页统一取辐角主值：归到 (−180°, 180°] 里的那一个。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：实部、虚部分别限制到 −5…5。这是图的范围，不是复数的数学范围。

z · 实部 Re
z · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

z 坐标未改变，保留当前精确值。

预设点巡演：
3 + 4i
−4（纯实数）
3i（纯虚数）
单位圆上 · 50°

z ≈ −2.3 + 1.8i：实部 a ≈ −2.3，虚部 b ≈ 1.8；模 |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 2.92（斜边由勾股实算）；辐角 θ ≈ 142°（从实轴正半轴逆时针量）。数字由未舍入坐标计算后显示为近似值。

结论：钉住一个点有两套办法——坐标 (a, b)，或者（模，辐角）。它们是同一根箭头的两种读法：前者说「向右走几、向上走几」，后者说「多长、朝哪个方向」。下一步加法用第一套读法最顺，乘法则要靠第二套——先都认熟。

边界逐个验：把点拖到负实轴上，辐角读作 +180° 而不是 −180°——主值区间的右端是闭的。拖到单位圆上（虚线圈）时模恒为 1，只剩角度在变；这时箭头尖的坐标正是 (cos θ, sin θ)，这个读法的出处在三角函数页第 1 步。

第 2 步 · 加法

加法 = 平移：和的坐标就是两边坐标各自相加

这一步要回答：两个复数相加，图上到底动了什么？图上有两根可拖的箭头 z₁、z₂，第三根绿箭头是它们的和 z₁ + z₂，用平行四边形法则画出（以 z₁、z₂ 为邻边张成平行四边形，对角线就是和；等价地看，z₂ 的箭头首尾相接到 z₁ 的尖端，落点相同）。拖任意一根，下面三栏对账会逐栏核对：和的实部、虚部是不是恰好两边各自相加。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：每个输入复数的两分量分别限制到 −4.2…4.2；和仍由两数实算。此范围只为绘图。

目标复数

z₁ · 第一个数
z₂ · 第二个数
z₁ · 实部 Re
z₁ · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

z₁ = −1.3 + 2.2i，z₂ = 2.7 − 0.8i，z₁ + z₂ = 1.4 + 1.4i

实部对账：−1.3 + 2.7 = 1.4 ✓（正是和的实部）

虚部对账：2.2 + −0.8 = 1.4 ✓（正是和的虚部）

结论：加 z₂，就是把整幅图沿 z₂ 这根箭头平移那么远；和的横、纵坐标恰是两边各自相加。这与向量加法是同一件事——复数加法 = 分量相加 = 平移，只对加法成立。

先埋一个反差：乘法不是分量相乘。(1 + i) × (1 + i) 若按分量乘会得 1 + 1i 之类怪东西，真实答案第 4 步在对账台上见——乘法动的是模和角，不是分量。

第 3 步 · 乘 i

乘 i：什么都不改，只转 90°

这一步要回答：i 自己到底「是」什么？选一个起点，按「× i」按钮连着按：每按一次，箭头就逆时针转 90°——盯住读数：模纹丝不动，辐角每次恰好 +90°（超过 180° 就按主值归回来）。落点和弧线全程留痕，连按四次，箭头回到原来的方向。下面还有一条单位点巡演：1 → i → −1 → −i → 1，落点逐个钉在坐标轴上。

起点 z：
1（单位点）
3 + 2i
× i（转 90°）
重置 ↺
已乘 i 4 次（每 4 次回到原方向）

当前 z = 3 + 2i：模 = 3.61（乘 i 前后一模一样）；辐角 = 33.7°。

转满一圈了：四次 90° 正好 360°，箭头回到起点方向——i 的幂以 4 为周期。

单位点巡演（全部由连乘实算）：i¹ = i，i² = −1，i³ = −i，i⁴ = 1。看 i² 落在哪：从 1 出发转两次 90° 就是掉头 180°，落在 −1 上。

收口：×i = 逆时针旋转 90°，所以 i² = 转两次 = 掉头 = −1。i² = −1 是转出来的，不是背出来的。「i 是 √−1 的记号」和「i 是转 90° 的动作」是同一个 i 的两副面孔：前者是它的名字，后者是它的行为。

换起点 3 + 2i 再连按四次：四个落点不在坐标轴上，但模始终是 √13、辐角每次 +90°、第四次严丝合缝回到 (3, 2)——周期 4 对任何起点都成立，因为转四次就是转一整圈。

第 4 步 · 一般乘法

一般乘法 = 模相乘、角相加：对账台

这一步要回答：乘上任意一个复数，模和角各发生什么？先把两件事分开验明：乘一个正实数（如下方预设 2）只伸缩不转；乘一个模为 1 的数只转不伸缩。任意乘数 z₂ 则是两件事叠加。拖动 z₁（被乘）与 z₂（乘数），绿箭头是乘积 z₁·z₂；下面对账台三组读数全部实算：模对账、角对账、还有一条代数路 (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂)——两条路同源互证。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：每个输入复数的模最多 2.6。吸附后超出圆盘时，按比例缩到圆周且不改方向；最终分量可能不在 0.1 网格上。此范围只为绘图。

试着用坐标把两数都设为 1+i：先预测乘积的模与辐角，再应用，对照图与下方读数。

目标复数

z₁ · 第一个数
z₂ · 第二个数
z₂ · 实部 Re
z₂ · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

已按吸附与绘图范围应用 z₂ = 1.56 + 2.08i；输入框已同步实际坐标。

把乘数 z₂ 换成预设：
2（纯实数 · 只伸缩）
模 1 · 60°（只旋转）
1 + i（转 45° 又放大 √2 倍）

符号恒等式是精确的；下方显示的分量和模最多保留 2 位小数、角度最多 1 位。请勿用舍入后的操作数回算精确等式。

z₁ ≈ −1.2 + 0.7i，z₂ ≈ 1.56 + 2.08i ⟹ z₁·z₂ ≈ −3.33 − 1.4i

模恒等式：|z₁z₂| = |z₁| × |z₂|。显示两因子模：|z₁| ≈ 1.39，|z₂| ≈ 2.6；用未舍入值相乘后显示 |z₁|·|z₂| ≈ 3.61，直接求乘积模得 |z₁z₂| ≈ 3.61。

角对账：显示 θ₁ ≈ 149.7°，θ₂ ≈ 53.1°；未舍入角相加并归到主值区间后 ≈ −157.1°，直接算乘积辐角 ≈ −157.1°。

代数恒等式：(a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂)。显示坐标：a₁ ≈ (−1.2)，b₁ ≈ 0.7，a₂ ≈ 1.56，b₂ ≈ 2.08；用未舍入坐标算乘积 ≈ −3.33 − 1.4i，图也使用同一结果。

结论：乘法法则——模相乘、角相加。乘上谁，就按谁的模伸缩、按谁的辐角旋转。条件写明：角度相加后必须按主值区间归一化（340° 与 −20° 是同一个方向，本页统一写 −20°）；乘数或被乘数是 0 时，乘积是原点、无辐角可言。

本演台把两个点限制在模 ≤ 2.6 的圆盘内，免得乘积跑出图外——法则本身对任意大小的复数都成立。先用预设 1 + i 验一组：z₁ = 2 + i 时乘积辐角应比原来恰好多 45°、模恰好多乘 √2，对账台会当场打勾。

第 5 步 · 自测

自测：转得对不对，当场验

三道题的判定都由与正文同源的实算给出：落点由连乘算、模由勾股算，不预设答案表。答对一题锁定一题（答题后去拖正文的点，不会冲掉这里的判定）；答错会按你的错法给出诊断，可以再试。

题 1 · 连乘两次 i

z = 3 + 2i，连乘两次 i（即 z·i²），落在哪里？先在心里转：一次 90°、再一次 90°。

3 − 2i
−3 − 2i
−3 + 2i
3 + 2i

✓ 对了：连乘两次 i 就是转 180° 掉头，(3, 2) 落到 −3 − 2i。顺带说，这正是 z·i² = −z 的几何样子。

题 2 · 谁的模大

|3 + 4i| 与 |−4 + 3i|，哪个大？别急着选——两个模都由勾股实算，算完再比。

3 + 4i 更大
−4 + 3i 更大
一样大

✓ 对：|3 + 4i| = 5，|−4 + 3i| = 5，相等。两个点方向不同、离原点的距离却一样——模只看长度，不看方向。

题 3 · 判断

判断这句话：「乘积的模，等于两个模之和。」

对
错

text:
← Knowledge Index

Complex Numbers · Multiplication Is Rotation Plus Scaling

In the textbook, i drops out of the sky: “define i² = −1”. You memorise it, you can compute with it, but you never learn what it is. This page tells it differently: first bring numbers back from a line onto a plane — a complex number (a number of the form a + bi, with a and b real) is a point on the plane, an arrow; addition slides the arrow, multiplication rotates and scales it. Then i² = −1 needs no memorising: multiplying by i is a 90° turn, and two turns point you exactly at −1. Every modulus, argument, sum and product on this page is computed on the spot from (a, b) alone — picture and readout share one source.

中
EN
0 The Line Is Not Enough
1 Points & Arrows
2 Addition Slides
3 ×i Turns 90°
4 Multiplication Bench
5 Self-Test
6 Finale

Step 0 · The Number Line Is Not Enough

The Number Line Is Not Enough: Where Does the Solution of x² = −1 Stand?

This step answers one question: the solution of x² = −1 — where does it stand? You already know: the real numbers fill a single line, and every real square is ≥ 0 — positive squared is positive, negative squared is positive, 0 squared is 0. The probe below lets you check by hand: drag x along the line and the trace above draws every value x² can take; it hugs the region above the line yet never reaches the −1 line. It is not hiding — there is simply no room for it on this line.

Square probe x (drag along the line) x = −1.5
Fold the plane away ↩

The plane is unfolded: the horizontal axis is still the original real axis; the newly raised one is the imaginary axis, and together they span the complex plane. The point one unit above the origin is the candidate to be claimed: this page now adopts it as i, and verifies step by step that its square really is −1 (the reveal is in Step 3).

Conclusion: x² = −1 has no real solution — what is missing is not a number but a dimension. Add a perpendicular axis to the line and numbers graduate from “points on a line” to “points on a plane”; the unit on the new axis is written i. For now just one promise: on this page i² = −1 becomes something you can see, not something you memorise.

Why a whole new axis, and not just one extra point? Because numbers must stay computable: the new point added to, and multiplied by, the old reals must have somewhere to land — only a whole plane holds the entire new number system. Next stop: learn to read “a point on the plane” fluently.

Start exploring ↓

Step 1 · A Point on the Complex Plane

A Complex Number Is a Point: Pin It by (a, b), or by (Modulus, Argument)

This step answers: how many numbers does it take to pin down one complex number? The picture is a complex plane: horizontal real axis, vertical imaginary axis. Drag the point z and all four readouts are computed live from its coordinates (a, b): a is the real part, b is the imaginary part (mind this: the imaginary part is the real number b itself, without the i), written z = a + bi; the arrow from the origin to z has length called the modulus |z| — the hypotenuse of Pythagoras’ theorem; the angle from the positive real axis, measured counter-clockwise, is the argument θ. Arguments have many equivalent writings; this page always uses the principal value: the one normalised into (−180°, 180°].

z ≈ −2.3 + 1.8i: real part a ≈ −2.3, imaginary part b ≈ 1.8; modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 2.92 (computed by Pythagoras); argument θ ≈ 142° (counter-clockwise from the positive real axis). Displayed numbers are rounded after calculation from unrounded coordinates.

Conclusion: there are two ways to pin the point — coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument). They are two readings of the same arrow: one says “how far right, how far up”, the other says “how long, pointing which way”. Addition next door reads most naturally in the first; multiplication will need the second — get fluent in both.

Check the boundaries one by one: drag the point onto the negative real axis and the argument reads +180°, not −180° — the right end of the principal interval is closed. On the unit circle (the dashed ring) the modulus stays 1 and only the angle moves; there the arrow tip’s coordinates are exactly (cos θ, sin θ) — that reading is established in Step 1 of the trigonometry page.

Step 2 · Addition

Addition = Sliding: the Sum’s Coordinates Are the Two Sides Added Separately

This step answers: when two complex numbers are added, what actually moves in the picture? Two draggable arrows z₁ and z₂ are on stage; the green arrow is their sum z₁ + z₂, drawn by the parallelogram rule (span a parallelogram with z₁, z₂ as adjacent sides and the diagonal is the sum; equivalently, attach z₂’s arrow head-to-tail at z₁’s tip — same landing point). Drag either arrow and the three check rows below verify, row by row, that the sum’s real and imaginary parts are exactly the two sides added separately.

Imaginary-part check: 2.2 + −0.8 = 1.4 ✓ (exactly the sum’s imaginary part)

Conclusion: adding z₂ slides the whole picture along z₂’s arrow by exactly that much; the sum’s horizontal and vertical coordinates are the two sides added separately. It is the same thing as vector addition — complex addition = component-wise addition = translation, and it holds for addition only.

Plant a contrast: multiplication is not component-wise. If (1 + i) × (1 + i) were multiplied component-wise you would get something odd like 1 + 1i; the true answer appears on the bench in Step 4 — multiplication moves modulus and angle, not components.

Step 3 · Multiply by i

Multiply by i: Nothing Changes Except a 90° Turn

This step answers: what is i, itself? Pick a starting point and keep pressing “× i”: each press turns the arrow 90° counter-clockwise — watch the readout: the modulus does not budge, the argument gains exactly +90° each time (wrapping back by the principal value past 180°). Landing points and arcs stay on stage the whole time; press four times and the arrow faces its original direction again. Below runs the unit-point tour: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1, landings pinned one by one on the axes.

Starting point z:
1 (the unit point)
3 + 2i
× i (turn 90°)
Reset ↺
Multiplied by i 4 times (every 4 turns restore the direction)

Current z = 3 + 2i: modulus = 3.61 (identical before and after ×i); argument = 33.7°.

A full turn: four 90° turns make 360°, and the arrow faces its starting direction again — the powers of i cycle with period 4.

The unit-point tour (all computed by repeated multiplication): i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Watch where i² lands: two 90° turns from 1 are a 180° about-face, landing on −1.

The verdict: ×i = a 90° counter-clockwise rotation, so i² = two turns = an about-face = −1. i² = −1 is turned into existence, not memorised into it. “i is the notation for √−1” and “i is the action of turning 90°” are two faces of the same i: the first is its name, the second is its behaviour.

Switch the start to 3 + 2i and press four more times: the landings are off-axis, yet the modulus stays √13 throughout, the argument gains 90° each press, and the fourth press lands exactly back on (3, 2) — period 4 holds for every start, because four turns are one full turn.

Step 4 · General Multiplication

General Multiplication = Moduli Multiply, Arguments Add: the Checking Bench

This step answers: multiplying by an arbitrary complex number — what happens to modulus and to angle? First verify the two halves separately: multiplying by a positive real (preset 2 below) only scales and never turns; multiplying by a number of modulus 1 only turns and never scales. An arbitrary multiplier z₂ stacks the two. Drag z₁ (the multiplicand) and z₂ (the multiplier); the green arrow is the product z₁·z₂. The bench below checks three groups, all computed live: the modulus check, the angle check, and an algebraic route (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂) — two roads, one source, cross-verified.

Self-Test: Turn It Right, Checked on the Spot

Get one right and it locks (dragging points in the main text afterwards will not wash the verdict away); get one wrong and the feedback diagnoses your exact wrong turn, and you may retry.

Question 1 · Multiply by i twice

z = 3 + 2i. Multiply by i twice (that is, z·i²) — where does it land? Turn it in your head first: 90° once, then 90° again.

3 − 2i
−3 − 2i
−3 + 2i
3 + 2i

✓ Correct: two multiplications by i are a 180° about-face, and (3, 2) lands on −3 − 2i. Incidentally, this is exactly what z·i² = −z looks like geometrically.

Question 2 · Whose modulus is bigger

|3 + 4i| versus |−4 + 3i| — which is bigger? Do not rush: both moduli are computed by Pythagoras; compute first, then compare.

3 + 4i is bigger
−4 + 3i is bigger
They are equal

✓ Correct: |3 + 4i| = 5 and |−4 + 3i| = 5 — equal. The two points point in different directions yet sit at the same distance from the origin: the modulus sees length only, never direction.

Question 3 · True or false

Judge this claim: “The modulus of a product equals the sum of the two moduli.”

True
False

✓ Correct judgment — the claim is false: test it on the spot with a ready-made set of numbers — with z₁ = z₂ = 1 + i, |z₁|·|z₂| = 2, exactly |(1 + i)²| = |2i| = 2; the “sum of moduli” would give 2.83, which does not match. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli, not the sum. You can also drag your own group on the Step 4 bench to re-verify.

The three, wrapped up: (1) multiplying by i twice is an about-face — both coordinates flip sign; (2) the modulus recognises length only: (3, 4) and (−4, 3) are the same Pythagorean pair, swapped and sign-flipped, both of modulus 5; (3) moduli multiply, arguments add — the “sum” lives on the angle side only; on the modulus side it is always a product.

Finale: One Plane, Two Operations

A complex number is a point on the plane

z = a + bi corresponds one-to-one with a point of the plane and with an arrow from the origin. Pin it two ways: coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument) — the modulus is the arrow’s length, the argument its direction (principal value (−180°, 180°] on this page).

Addition is sliding

The sum’s coordinates are the two sides’ coordinates added separately; in the picture it is one slide along the added number’s arrow — the diagonal of the parallelogram. Addition moves position only.

Multiplication is rotation + scaling

Moduli multiply, arguments add: multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Multiplying by i is the purest case — modulus 1, angle 90°, rotation with no scaling; and i² = −1 is simply “two turns make an about-face”.

One sentence each for two roads ahead: division is the inverse of multiplication — arguments subtract, moduli divide — not expanded on this page. And one planted thread: if this point starts turning on its own, its angle growing uniformly with time, its position is eiθ running on the unit circle — the doorway to Euler’s formula, named here only.

Complex Numbers · Multiplication Is Rotation Plus Scaling

In the textbook, i drops out of the sky: “define i² = −1”. You memorise it, you can compute with it, but you never learn what it is. This page tells it differently: first bring numbers back from a line onto a plane — a complex number (a number of the form a + bi, with a and b real) is a point on the plane, an arrow; addition slides the arrow, multiplication rotates and scales it. Then i² = −1 needs no memorising: multiplying by i is a 90° turn, and two turns point you exactly at −1. Every modulus, argument, sum and product on this page is computed on the spot from (a, b) alone — picture and readout share one source.

Step 0 · The Number Line Is Not Enough

The Number Line Is Not Enough: Where Does the Solution of x² = −1 Stand?

This step answers one question: the solution of x² = −1 — where does it stand? You already know: the real numbers fill a single line, and every real square is ≥ 0 — positive squared is positive, negative squared is positive, 0 squared is 0. The probe below lets you check by hand: drag x along the line and the trace above draws every value x² can take; it hugs the region above the line yet never reaches the −1 line. It is not hiding — there is simply no room for it on this line.

Square probe x (drag along the line) x = 1
Stand the line up as one edge: unfold the plane ⤢

Probe x = 1: x² = 1 ≥ 0. Drag x from negative to positive and the square traces a parabola whose lowest point is 0 — a whole unreachable gap away from −1.

Conclusion: x² = −1 has no real solution — what is missing is not a number but a dimension. Add a perpendicular axis to the line and numbers graduate from “points on a line” to “points on a plane”; the unit on the new axis is written i. For now just one promise: on this page i² = −1 becomes something you can see, not something you memorise.

Why a whole new axis, and not just one extra point? Because numbers must stay computable: the new point added to, and multiplied by, the old reals must have somewhere to land — only a whole plane holds the entire new number system. Next stop: learn to read “a point on the plane” fluently.

Start exploring ↓

Step 1 · A Point on the Complex Plane

A Complex Number Is a Point: Pin It by (a, b), or by (Modulus, Argument)

This step answers: how many numbers does it take to pin down one complex number? The picture is a complex plane: horizontal real axis, vertical imaginary axis. Drag the point z and all four readouts are computed live from its coordinates (a, b): a is the real part, b is the imaginary part (mind this: the imaginary part is the real number b itself, without the i), written z = a + bi; the arrow from the origin to z has length called the modulus |z| — the hypotenuse of Pythagoras’ theorem; the angle from the positive real axis, measured counter-clockwise, is the argument θ. Arguments have many equivalent writings; this page always uses the principal value: the one normalised into (−180°, 180°].

z ≈ 3 + 4i: real part a ≈ 3, imaginary part b ≈ 4; modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 5 (computed by Pythagoras); argument θ ≈ 53.1° (counter-clockwise from the positive real axis). Displayed numbers are rounded after calculation from unrounded coordinates.

Conclusion: there are two ways to pin the point — coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument). They are two readings of the same arrow: one says “how far right, how far up”, the other says “how long, pointing which way”. Addition next door reads most naturally in the first; multiplication will need the second — get fluent in both.

Check the boundaries one by one: drag the point onto the negative real axis and the argument reads +180°, not −180° — the right end of the principal interval is closed. On the unit circle (the dashed ring) the modulus stays 1 and only the angle moves; there the arrow tip’s coordinates are exactly (cos θ, sin θ) — that reading is established in Step 1 of the trigonometry page.

Step 2 · Addition

Addition = Sliding: the Sum’s Coordinates Are the Two Sides Added Separately

This step answers: when two complex numbers are added, what actually moves in the picture? Two draggable arrows z₁ and z₂ are on stage; the green arrow is their sum z₁ + z₂, drawn by the parallelogram rule (span a parallelogram with z₁, z₂ as adjacent sides and the diagonal is the sum; equivalently, attach z₂’s arrow head-to-tail at z₁’s tip — same landing point). Drag either arrow and the three check rows below verify, row by row, that the sum’s real and imaginary parts are exactly the two sides added separately.

Conclusion: adding z₂ slides the whole picture along z₂’s arrow by exactly that much; the sum’s horizontal and vertical coordinates are the two sides added separately. Step 3 · Multiply by i

Multiply by i: Nothing Changes Except a 90° Turn

This step answers: what is i, itself? Pick a starting point and keep pressing “× i”: each press turns the arrow 90° counter-clockwise — watch the readout: the modulus does not budge, the argument gains exactly +90° each time (wrapping back by the principal value past 180°). Landing points and arcs stay on stage the whole time; press four times and the arrow faces its original direction again. Below runs the unit-point tour: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1, landings pinned one by one on the axes.

Starting point z:
1 (the unit point)
3 + 2i
× i (turn 90°)
Reset ↺
Multiplied by i 0 times (every 4 turns restore the direction)

Current z = 1: modulus = 1 (identical before and after ×i); argument = 0°.

The unit-point tour (all computed by repeated multiplication): i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Watch where i² lands: two 90° turns from 1 are a 180° about-face, landing on −1.

The verdict: ×i = a 90° counter-clockwise rotation, so i² = two turns = an about-face = −1. i² = −1 is turned into existence, not memorised into it. “i is the notation for √−1” and “i is the action of turning 90°” are two faces of the same i: the first is its name, the second is its behaviour.

Switch the start to 3 + 2i and press four more times: the landings are off-axis, yet the modulus stays √13 throughout, the argument gains 90° each press, and the fourth press lands exactly back on (3, 2) — period 4 holds for every start, because four turns are one full turn.

text:
Step 6 · Finale

Finale: One Plane, Two Operations

Complex numbers are not a rule to memorise — they are the arithmetic that grows naturally once numbers are put back on the plane. Three closing cards:

A complex number is a point on the plane

z = a + bi corresponds one-to-one with a point of the plane and with an arrow from the origin. Pin it two ways: coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument) — the modulus is the arrow’s length, the argument its direction (principal value (−180°, 180°] on this page).

Addition is sliding

The sum’s coordinates are the two sides’ coordinates added separately; in the picture it is one slide along the added number’s arrow — the diagonal of the parallelogram. Addition moves position only.

Multiplication is rotation + scaling

Moduli multiply, arguments add: multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Multiplying by i is the purest case — modulus 1, angle 90°, rotation with no scaling; and i² = −1 is simply “two turns make an about-face”.

One sentence each for two roads ahead: division is the inverse of multiplication — arguments subtract, moduli divide — not expanded on this page. And one planted thread: if this point starts turning on its own, its angle growing uniformly with time, its position is eiθ running on the unit circle — the doorway to Euler’s formula, named here only.

The very point at angle θ, set turning and with its height unrolled, is the sine wave — watch it move on the trigonometry page →

← 知识索引

复数 · 乘法是旋转加伸缩

课本里 i 是空降的：「规定 i² = −1」，背下来、会算、但不知道它是什么。这一页换个讲法：先把数从一条线请回一张平面——复数（形如 a + bi 的数，a、b 都是实数）就是平面上的一个点、一根箭头；加法是把箭头平移，乘法是把箭头旋转加伸缩。于是 i² = −1 不必背：乘 i 就是转 90°，转两次正好掉头指向 −1。这一页所有的模、辐角、和、积，都只由 (a, b) 当场实算，图和读数同源。

中
EN
0 数轴不够用
1 点与箭头
2 加法是平移
3 乘 i 转 90°
4 乘法对账台
5 自测
6 终章

第 0 步 · 数轴不够用

数轴不够用：x² = −1 的解站在哪里？

这一步要回答：方程 x² = −1 的解，到底站在哪里？你已经知道：实数全排在一条数轴上，而任何实数的平方都 ≥ 0——正数平方是正数，负数平方也是正数，0 的平方是 0。下面这台探针让你亲手验：拖着 x 沿数轴走，上方描出的轨迹是 x² 的全部取值，它贴着数轴上方走，却永远够不到 −1 那条横线。找不到不是因为没找仔细——是这条线上根本没有它的位置。

平方探针 x（沿数轴拖） x = 1
把数轴竖起来当一条边：展开平面 ⤢

探针 x = 1：x² = 1 ≥ 0。把 x 从负拖到正，平方一路描出一条抛物线，最低点就是 0——离 −1 还差着整整一条「够不到」的距离。

结论：x² = −1 在实数里无解，缺的不是某个数、是一个维度。给数轴加一条垂直的轴，数就从「线上的点」升级为「平面上的点」；新轴上的单位记作 i。这一步先只承诺一件事：i² = −1 在本页会变成看得见的事实，不靠背。

为什么非得加一整条轴，而不是只添一个点？因为数要能运算：添进来的点和原来的实数相加、相乘，结果还得有地方站——一张平面才装得下这一整套新数。下一站先把「平面上的点」这套读法认全。

开始探索 ↓

第 1 步 · 复平面上的点

复数是平面上的点：钉住它要么 (a, b)，要么（模，辐角）

这一步要回答：一个复数，要几个数才能钉住？图上是一个复平面：横轴是实轴、纵轴是虚轴。拖动点 z，读数四栏全部由它的坐标 (a, b) 当场实算：a 叫实部、b 叫虚部（注意：虚部是 b 这个实数本身，不带 i），写法记作 z = a + bi；从原点向 z 拉出的箭头，长度叫模 |z|——就是勾股定理里那根斜边；箭头与实轴正半轴的夹角（逆时针量）叫辐角 θ。辐角有很多个等价写法，本页统一取辐角主值：归到 (−180°, 180°] 里的那一个。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：实部、虚部分别限制到 −5…5。这是图的范围，不是复数的数学范围。

z · 实部 Re
z · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

预设点巡演：
3 + 4i
−4（纯实数）
3i（纯虚数）
单位圆上 · 50°

z ≈ 3 + 4i：实部 a ≈ 3，虚部 b ≈ 4；模 |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 5（斜边由勾股实算）；辐角 θ ≈ 53.1°（从实轴正半轴逆时针量）。数字由未舍入坐标计算后显示为近似值。

结论：钉住一个点有两套办法——坐标 (a, b)，或者（模，辐角）。它们是同一根箭头的两种读法：前者说「向右走几、向上走几」，后者说「多长、朝哪个方向」。下一步加法用第一套读法最顺，乘法则要靠第二套——先都认熟。

边界逐个验：把点拖到负实轴上，辐角读作 +180° 而不是 −180°——主值区间的右端是闭的。拖到单位圆上（虚线圈）时模恒为 1，只剩角度在变；这时箭头尖的坐标正是 (cos θ, sin θ)，这个读法的出处在三角函数页第 1 步。

第 2 步 · 加法

加法 = 平移：和的坐标就是两边坐标各自相加

这一步要回答：两个复数相加，图上到底动了什么？图上有两根可拖的箭头 z₁、z₂，第三根绿箭头是它们的和 z₁ + z₂，用平行四边形法则画出（以 z₁、z₂ 为邻边张成平行四边形，对角线就是和；等价地看，z₂ 的箭头首尾相接到 z₁ 的尖端，落点相同）。拖任意一根，下面三栏对账会逐栏核对：和的实部、虚部是不是恰好两边各自相加。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：每个输入复数的两分量分别限制到 −4.2…4.2；和仍由两数实算。此范围只为绘图。

目标复数

z₁ · 第一个数
z₂ · 第二个数
z₁ · 实部 Re
z₁ · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

z₁ = 2 + i，z₂ = 1 + 2i，z₁ + z₂ = 3 + 3i

实部对账：2 + 1 = 3 ✓（正是和的实部）

虚部对账：1 + 2 = 3 ✓（正是和的虚部）

结论：加 z₂，就是把整幅图沿 z₂ 这根箭头平移那么远；和的横、纵坐标恰是两边各自相加。这与向量加法是同一件事——复数加法 = 分量相加 = 平移，只对加法成立。

先埋一个反差：乘法不是分量相乘。(1 + i) × (1 + i) 若按分量乘会得 1 + 1i 之类怪东西，真实答案第 4 步在对账台上见——乘法动的是模和角，不是分量。

第 3 步 · 乘 i

乘 i：什么都不改，只转 90°

这一步要回答：i 自己到底「是」什么？选一个起点，按「× i」按钮连着按：每按一次，箭头就逆时针转 90°——盯住读数：模纹丝不动，辐角每次恰好 +90°（超过 180° 就按主值归回来）。落点和弧线全程留痕，连按四次，箭头回到原来的方向。下面还有一条单位点巡演：1 → i → −1 → −i → 1，落点逐个钉在坐标轴上。

起点 z：
1（单位点）
3 + 2i
× i（转 90°）
重置 ↺
已乘 i 0 次（每 4 次回到原方向）

当前 z = 1：模 = 1（乘 i 前后一模一样）；辐角 = 0°。

单位点巡演（全部由连乘实算）：i¹ = i，i² = −1，i³ = −i，i⁴ = 1。看 i² 落在哪：从 1 出发转两次 90° 就是掉头 180°，落在 −1 上。

收口：×i = 逆时针旋转 90°，所以 i² = 转两次 = 掉头 = −1。i² = −1 是转出来的，不是背出来的。「i 是 √−1 的记号」和「i 是转 90° 的动作」是同一个 i 的两副面孔：前者是它的名字，后者是它的行为。

换起点 3 + 2i 再连按四次：四个落点不在坐标轴上，但模始终是 √13、辐角每次 +90°、第四次严丝合缝回到 (3, 2)——周期 4 对任何起点都成立，因为转四次就是转一整圈。

第 4 步 · 一般乘法

一般乘法 = 模相乘、角相加：对账台

这一步要回答：乘上任意一个复数，模和角各发生什么？先把两件事分开验明：乘一个正实数（如下方预设 2）只伸缩不转；乘一个模为 1 的数只转不伸缩。任意乘数 z₂ 则是两件事叠加。拖动 z₁（被乘）与 z₂（乘数），绿箭头是乘积 z₁·z₂；下面对账台三组读数全部实算：模对账、角对账、还有一条代数路 (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂)——两条路同源互证。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：每个输入复数的模最多 2.6。吸附后超出圆盘时，按比例缩到圆周且不改方向；最终分量可能不在 0.1 网格上。此范围只为绘图。

试着用坐标把两数都设为 1+i：先预测乘积的模与辐角，再应用，对照图与下方读数。

目标复数

z₁ · 第一个数
z₂ · 第二个数
z₂ · 实部 Re
z₂ · 虚部 Im（不含 i）
应用坐标

把乘数 z₂ 换成预设：
2（纯实数 · 只伸缩）
模 1 · 60°（只旋转）
1 + i（转 45° 又放大 √2 倍）

符号恒等式是精确的；下方显示的分量和模最多保留 2 位小数、角度最多 1 位。请勿用舍入后的操作数回算精确等式。

z₁ ≈ 2 + i，z₂ ≈ 1 + i ⟹ z₁·z₂ ≈ 1 + 3i

模恒等式：|z₁z₂| = |z₁| × |z₂|。显示两因子模：|z₁| ≈ 2.24，|z₂| ≈ 1.41；用未舍入值相乘后显示 |z₁|·|z₂| ≈ 3.16，直接求乘积模得 |z₁z₂| ≈ 3.16。

角对账：显示 θ₁ ≈ 26.6°，θ₂ ≈ 45°；未舍入角相加并归到主值区间后 ≈ 71.6°，直接算乘积辐角 ≈ 71.6°。

代数恒等式：(a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂)。显示坐标：a₁ ≈ 2，b₁ ≈ 1，a₂ ≈ 1，b₂ ≈ 1；用未舍入坐标算乘积 ≈ 1 + 3i，图也使用同一结果。

结论：乘法法则——模相乘、角相加。乘上谁，就按谁的模伸缩、按谁的辐角旋转。条件写明：角度相加后必须按主值区间归一化（340° 与 −20° 是同一个方向，本页统一写 −20°）；乘数或被乘数是 0 时，乘积是原点、无辐角可言。

本演台把两个点限制在模 ≤ 2.6 的圆盘内，免得乘积跑出图外——法则本身对任意大小的复数都成立。先用预设 1 + i 验一组：z₁ = 2 + i 时乘积辐角应比原来恰好多 45°、模恰好多乘 √2，对账台会当场打勾。

第 5 步 · 自测

自测：转得对不对，当场验

三道题的判定都由与正文同源的实算给出：落点由连乘算、模由勾股算，不预设答案表。答对一题锁定一题（答题后去拖正文的点，不会冲掉这里的判定）；答错会按你的错法给出诊断，可以再试。

题 1 · 连乘两次 i

z = 3 + 2i，连乘两次 i（即 z·i²），落在哪里？先在心里转：一次 90°、再一次 90°。

−3 + 2i
3 − 2i
3 + 2i
−3 − 2i

题 2 · 谁的模大

|3 + 4i| 与 |−4 + 3i|，哪个大？别急着选——两个模都由勾股实算，算完再比。

3 + 4i 更大
−4 + 3i 更大
一样大

题 3 · 判断

判断这句话：「乘积的模，等于两个模之和。」

对
错

第 6 步 · 终章

终章：一张平面，两种运算

复数不是一条要背的法则，是把数放回平面之后自然长出来的运算。收口三张卡：

复数是平面上的点

z = a + bi 与平面上的点、与从原点出发的箭头一一对应。钉住它有两种读法：坐标 (a, b)，或（模，辐角）——模是箭头的长度，辐角是它的方向（本页取主值 (−180°, 180°]）。

加法是平移

和的坐标 = 两边坐标各自相加，图上就是沿着加数的箭头平移一次——平行四边形的对角线。加法只动位置，不动方向和长度的读法。

乘法是旋转 + 伸缩

模相乘、角相加：乘上谁，就按谁的模伸缩、按谁的辐角旋转。乘 i 是其中最纯粹的一例——模 1、角 90°，只转不伸缩；i² = −1 就是「转两次正好掉头」。

两个方向先各留一句话：除法是乘法的逆——角相减、模相除，本页不展开。再往前一步埋一条线：如果这个点自己转起来、角度随时间均匀长大，它的位置就是 eiθ 在单位圆上跑——那是欧拉公式的入口，本页只点名。

辐角 θ 的那个点转起来、把身高摊开，就是正弦波——去三角函数页看它动起来 →

第 6 步 · 终章

稳态：λ = 1 的特征向量，与谷歌的起点

最后一站，一张 4 个节点的小网：A、B、C、D 互相指着箭头。想象每个节点上站着一群人，每一步，每个人都沿出箭头均匀随机地走到下个节点——这就是马尔可夫链，转移矩阵 M 的每一列写明「从这一列的节点出发，落到各行的概率」，所以每列之和必须恰好是 1（人不会凭空消失）。从任意初始分布出发，反复乘 M：分布一步步变，最后冻住不动——冻住的分布 π 满足 Mπ = π，它正是 M 的一个特征向量，特征值恰好 λ = 1。点「换初始分布」再跑：起点天差地别，终点分毫不差。谷歌的 PageRank 就是把整个互联网当成这张图：稳态分布即网页排名（真实 PageRank 还加了阻尼：每步以 0.15 的概率随机跳到任意页，公式 π ← 0.85·Mπ + 0.15/N，保证链一定收敛；本页的小网本身可达且无周期，不加阻尼也收敛）。

PageRank：稳态即排名

把网页看成节点、链接看成箭头，PageRank 求的就是这张巨图的 λ = 1 特征向量：稳态分量最大的网页最重要。求法还是第 3 步的幂迭代——乘到不动为止。

振动模态：特征频率

桥梁和建筑的振动方程里，特征向量是振型（各部位摆动的相对幅值），特征值给出固有频率。工程师避开共振、抗震设计，算的全是特征问题。

稳定性：回到单位圆

离散系统 x ← Ax 稳定 ⟺ A 的全部特征值 |λ| < 1 —— 与 Z 变换页里「极点在单位圆内才稳定」是同一句话：系统矩阵的特征值，就是极点的真身。链接：Z 变换。

从捏圆的机器到谷歌的排名，中间只隔一个问题：「哪个方向不会被转走？」特征向量是矩阵的骨架——看懂了骨架，拉伸、旋转、振动、数据的形状、网络的稳态，全都是同一件事的不同说法。

第 2 步 · 特征值的性格

四个数随便调，λ 当场改命

这一站把矩阵的四个数 a、b、c、d 全交给你。λ₁、λ₂ 和两条特征方向线实时重算，旁边并排摆着两条恒等式：λ₁ + λ₂ 必须等于迹 tr A = a + d，λ₁λ₂ 必须等于行列式 det A——误差在 10⁻¹⁵ 量级，是浮点数最后的倔强。挨个点一遍预设巡演：负特征值把箭头翻过去；两个 λ 都小于 1 时圆整体缩水；剪切矩阵只有一个特征方向（重根、亏损，老实只画一条）；旋转缩放判别式小于零，实特征方向压根不存在——λ 是一对共轭复数，页面绝不画假方向给你，只给你看真实行为：一圈一圈的螺旋。

λ = (tr A ± √( (a−d)² + 4bc )) / 2，判别式 Δ = (a−d)² + 4bc

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors · The Directions a Matrix Won’t Turn

A matrix is a stretching machine: applied to space, it turns almost every arrow — except a few special directions that only get stretched, shrunk, or flipped, their line never bending. Those directions are eigenvectors; the stretch factors are eigenvalues. We start with a circle squeezed into an ellipse, drag the unturned directions out by hand, and end at the λ = 1 hiding behind Google’s ranking.

Step 0 · The Hook

A circle squeezed into an ellipse — two directions refuse to turn

Twenty arrows stand evenly on the unit circle. Apply the matrix A once: the circle is squeezed into an ellipse and the arrows are, almost all of them, turned. But watch the orange and pink pairs: they only grow or shrink — their line does not bend at all. Drag the slider to push the deformation back and forth between “circle” and “ellipse”. The whole plane is being twisted, so why do exactly these two directions stay put? This page investigates them.

A = [[2.2, 0.6], [0.6, 1.0]] (fixed for this step; every matrix on this page is 2×2 like this)

Morph t (0 = untouched, 1 = A fully applied) 1.00
Play the morph

Symbols first: λ (lambda) is the symbol for the eigenvalue — the orange direction: stretched by λ₁ ≈ 2.45 · Pink direction: shrunk to λ₂ ≈ 0.75 · Every other arrow: stretched and turned

Memorize the test: v is an eigenvector exactly when Av is collinear with v (same or opposite direction); the signed multiple is the eigenvalue λ. Next step, you drag an arrow yourself until it lines up.

Start exploring ↓

Step 1 · Hands On

Drag an arrow until it stops turning

The cyan arrow v is yours to drag (grab its tip, or press and drag anywhere). The orange arrow is Av — what the matrix does to it. Their angle is computed live: nonzero means v got turned; rotate v until it is exactly collinear with Av — same direction, or exactly opposite — and the angle hits zero: you have found an eigenvector. Opposite counts, too: then λ is negative and Av is v extended backwards. The curve below maps “direction angle θ → angle between v and Av” for every direction: it touches zero in exactly two places, the hiding spots of the two eigendirections.

Av = λv — v is an eigenvector, λ its eigenvalue

Matrix preset:
A classic symmetric [[2,1],[1,2]]
A general [[3,0.5],[0.5,1]]
A with a negative λ [[0.5,1.5],[1.5,0.5]]

Direction θ = 19.3° · angle(v, Av) = 16.59° · |Av| / |v| = 2.738 · signed stretch (v·Av)/|v|² = 2.624

Why exactly two zeros? The eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix are the two roots of λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0 (next step). The discriminant decides their character: two real roots, one repeated root, or a complex-conjugate pair — the whole personality of a matrix is written in that discriminant.

Step 2 · The Character of λ

All four entries are yours — watch λ change its fate

This step hands you all four entries a, b, c, d. λ₁, λ₂ and the two eigendirection lines are recomputed live, next to two identities: λ₁ + λ₂ must equal the trace tr A = a + d, and λ₁λ₂ must equal the determinant — the residuals hover around 10⁻¹⁵, floating point’s last stand. Tour the presets: a negative eigenvalue flips its arrow; both λ below 1 shrink the whole circle; the shear has only one eigendirection (a repeated, defective root — the page honestly draws just one line); the rotation–scaling has discriminant below zero, so real eigendirections do not exist — λ is a complex-conjugate pair, and the page will not fake a direction for you; it shows the true behavior instead: a spiral.

λ = (tr A ± √( (a−d)² + 4bc )) / 2, discriminant Δ = (a−d)² + 4bc

discriminant Δ = −3.633
λ = 0.550 ± 0.953i
|λ| = 1.100

Δ < 0: the eigenvalues are a complex-conjugate pair λ = α ± βi = 0.550 ± 0.953i, and there is no real eigendirection at all. The true behavior is rotation + scaling: each application turns vectors by 60.0° and multiplies lengths by 1.100.

How to read a negative λ: λ = −1 does not mean “shrunk by −1×”; it means flip the direction, then scale by |λ|. You already dragged one in Step 1’s third preset. Complex λ is not broken math either: it honestly reports a rotation hiding inside the transformation — bridges, AC circuits and quantum mechanics are full of complex eigenvalues.

Step 3 · Power Iteration

Multiply a hundred times — the main direction surfaces on its own

No idea where the eigenvector hides? Use the blunt method: multiply any vector by A, over and over. Each multiplication nudges the result closer to the dominant eigendirection (the one with largest |λ|), because the component along it grows by |λ₁| per step while the rest grows only by |λ₂| — the relative gap widens by a factor |λ₂/λ₁| each step. Push the ratio slider from 0.33 to 0.95: the closer the two eigenvalues, the slower the crawl, and the error curve grows a long tail. Then try the equal-modulus counterexample: with λ₂ = −λ₁ neither component can dominate, the vector hops between two directions forever and never converges — power iteration’s failure mode, labeled as such, never faked.

x ← Ax / |Ax|, repeat — x creeps toward the eigenvector of largest |λ|

The error is multiplied by roughly |λ₂/λ₁| each step — which is why r = 0.95 has such a long tail: 0.95¹⁰⁰ is still 0.006. Numerical libraries and Google’s PageRank find their eigenvectors with exactly this iteration (plus acceleration tricks). You will meet it once more in the finale.

Step 4 · Symmetric Matrices

Principal axes, orthogonality, diagonalization — the canyon’s true form

Symmetric matrices (b = c) enjoy a privilege: you can always choose a perpendicular pair of eigenvectors (when the two eigenvalues differ, the eigenvectors are perpendicular automatically — no choice involved; when an eigenvalue repeats, its eigenspace is a whole plane, and a perpendicular pair can still be picked from it). Overlaid are the contour ellipses of the quadratic form xᵀAx — remember the canyon from Step 2 of the Gradient Descent page? The ellipse’s long and short axes are exactly the two eigendirections, and the condition number κ = λmax/λmin is the canyon’s aspect ratio; here the eigenvalues appear in their true form. Press “Rotate into the eigenbasis”: the whole picture turns by θ until the eigendirections line up with the axes, and the matrix readout changes — the cross term vanishes, A becomes the diagonal Λ in the new coordinates, and QΛQᵀ reconstructs A with max entry error around 10⁻¹⁶: diagonalization is an identity, not an approximation.

Gradient descent zigzags in the canyon essentially because the coordinate axes are misaligned with the eigendirections: in the eigenbasis each direction takes its own step size and the zigzag vanishes. “Change the basis until the matrix is diagonal” is linear algebra’s most productive move — Step 5’s data compression and Step 6’s steady state both run on it. Link: see the zig-zag itself in the canyon →.

Step 5 · Principal Components of Data

The direction of maximum variance is the top eigenvector

An elongated cloud of 60 points (fixed random seed, already mean-centered). Drag the axis through the origin and read the sample variance of the data projected onto it (covariance convention: divide by n − 1, used consistently throughout this step) — the variance rises and falls as you turn, and its maximum is attained exactly at the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix. Press “Show principal components” and let it align itself: PC1 captures the share λ₁/(λ₁ + λ₂) of the total variance, PC2 is perpendicular to it and governed by λ₂. Rotate the data into this new basis and throw away the small axis, and the data is compressed — that is the whole of PCA (principal component analysis). How this principal direction is used in Kalman: velocity from position alone →

Covariance C = (1/(n−1)) Σ pᵢpᵢᵀ; eigenvectors of C = principal directions, eigenvalues = variance along them

Show principal components

Axis angle = 8.5° · sample variance along axis = 2.339 (the ceiling is λ₁ = 2.844)

Why does the max-variance direction deserve to be “principal”? Because the data spreads widest along it and carries the most information there; discarding the small perpendicular variance loses the least. Photo compression, face recognition (eigenfaces), financial risk factors — all run on this step’s covariance eigendecomposition.

Step 6 · Finale

The steady state: the λ = 1 eigenvector, and Google’s starting point

Final stop: a tiny four-node web — A, B, C, D pointing arrows at each other. Imagine a crowd standing on the nodes; at every step each person walks along an outgoing arrow, chosen uniformly at random. That is a Markov chain. Its transition matrix M has, in each column, the probabilities of leaving that column’s node for each row — so every column sums to exactly 1 (nobody vanishes). Start from any distribution and keep multiplying by M: the distribution shifts, then freezes — and a frozen distribution π satisfies Mπ = π: it is an eigenvector of M with eigenvalue exactly λ = 1. Switch the initial distribution and run again: wildly different starts, identical finish. Google’s PageRank treats the whole web as this graph, and the steady distribution is the ranking (real PageRank adds damping: at each step a 0.15 chance of teleporting to a random page, π ← 0.85·Mπ + 0.15/N, to guarantee convergence; this little web is reachable and aperiodic, so it converges undamped).

One λ, three faces
PageRank: the steady state is the ranking

Treat pages as nodes and links as arrows, and PageRank is the λ = 1 eigenvector of that giant graph: the page with the largest steady-state share is the most important. It is computed by Step 3’s power iteration — multiply until nothing moves.

Vibration modes: eigenfrequencies

In the vibration equations of bridges and buildings, eigenvectors are the mode shapes (relative sway of each part) and eigenvalues give the natural frequencies. Resonance avoidance and seismic design are, at bottom, eigenvalue problems.

Stability: back to the unit circle

A discrete system x ← Ax is stable ⟺ every eigenvalue satisfies |λ| < 1 — the same sentence as the Z-Transform page’s “poles inside the unit circle”: the system matrix’s eigenvalues ARE the poles. Link: The Z-Transform.

From the circle-squeezing machine to Google’s ranking, there is only one question in between: “which direction refuses to be turned?” Eigenvectors are a matrix’s skeleton — once you see the skeleton, stretching, rotation, vibration, the shape of data and the steady state of a network are all the same story told in different accents.

Step 6 · Finale

Finale: One Plane, Two Operations

Complex numbers are not a rule to memorise — they are the arithmetic that grows naturally once numbers are put back on the plane. Three closing cards:

A complex number is a point on the plane

z = a + bi corresponds one-to-one with a point of the plane and with an arrow from the origin. Pin it two ways: coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument) — the modulus is the arrow’s length, the argument its direction (principal value (−180°, 180°] on this page).

Addition is sliding

The sum’s coordinates are the two sides’ coordinates added separately; in the picture it is one slide along the added number’s arrow — the diagonal of the parallelogram. Addition moves position only.

Multiplication is rotation + scaling

Moduli multiply, arguments add: multiplying by a number scales you by its modulus and rotates you by its argument. Multiplying by i is the purest case — modulus 1, angle 90°, rotation with no scaling; and i² = −1 is simply “two turns make an about-face”.

One sentence each for two roads ahead: division is the inverse of multiplication — arguments subtract, moduli divide — not expanded on this page. And one planted thread: if this point starts turning on its own, its angle growing uniformly with time, its position is eiθ running on the unit circle — the doorway to Euler’s formula, named here only.

← Knowledge Index

Complex Numbers · Multiplication Is Rotation Plus Scaling

In the textbook, i drops out of the sky: “define i² = −1”. You memorise it, you can compute with it, but you never learn what it is. This page tells it differently: first bring numbers back from a line onto a plane — a complex number (a number of the form a + bi, with a and b real) is a point on the plane, an arrow; addition slides the arrow, multiplication rotates and scales it. Then i² = −1 needs no memorising: multiplying by i is a 90° turn, and two turns point you exactly at −1. Every modulus, argument, sum and product on this page is computed on the spot from (a, b) alone — picture and readout share one source.

Step 0 · The Number Line Is Not Enough

The Number Line Is Not Enough: Where Does the Solution of x² = −1 Stand?

This step answers one question: the solution of x² = −1 — where does it stand? You already know: the real numbers fill a single line, and every real square is ≥ 0 — positive squared is positive, negative squared is positive, 0 squared is 0. The probe below lets you check by hand: drag x along the line and the trace above draws every value x² can take; it hugs the region above the line yet never reaches the −1 line. It is not hiding — there is simply no room for it on this line.

Square probe x (drag along the line) x = 1
Stand the line up as one edge: unfold the plane ⤢

Probe x = 1: x² = 1 ≥ 0. Drag x from negative to positive and the square traces a parabola whose lowest point is 0 — a whole unreachable gap away from −1.

Conclusion: x² = −1 has no real solution — what is missing is not a number but a dimension. Add a perpendicular axis to the line and numbers graduate from “points on a line” to “points on a plane”; the unit on the new axis is written i. For now just one promise: on this page i² = −1 becomes something you can see, not something you memorise.

Why a whole new axis, and not just one extra point? Because numbers must stay computable: the new point added to, and multiplied by, the old reals must have somewhere to land — only a whole plane holds the entire new number system. Next stop: learn to read “a point on the plane” fluently.

Start exploring ↓

Step 1 · A Point on the Complex Plane

A Complex Number Is a Point: Pin It by (a, b), or by (Modulus, Argument)

This step answers: how many numbers does it take to pin down one complex number? The picture is a complex plane: horizontal real axis, vertical imaginary axis. Drag the point z and all four readouts are computed live from its coordinates (a, b): a is the real part, b is the imaginary part (mind this: the imaginary part is the real number b itself, without the i), written z = a + bi; the arrow from the origin to z has length called the modulus |z| — the hypotenuse of Pythagoras’ theorem; the angle from the positive real axis, measured counter-clockwise, is the argument θ. Arguments have many equivalent writings; this page always uses the principal value: the one normalised into (−180°, 180°].

Conclusion: there are two ways to pin the point — coordinates (a, b), or (modulus, argument). They are two readings of the same arrow: one says “how far right, how far up”, the other says “how long, pointing which way”. Addition next door reads most naturally in the first; multiplication will need the second — get fluent in both.

Check the boundaries one by one: drag the point onto the negative real axis and the argument reads +180°, not −180° — the right end of the principal interval is closed. On the unit circle (the dashed ring) the modulus stays 1 and only the angle moves; there the arrow tip’s coordinates are exactly (cos θ, sin θ) — that reading is established in Step 1 of the trigonometry page.

Step 2 · Addition

Addition = Sliding: the Sum’s Coordinates Are the Two Sides Added Separately

This step answers: when two complex numbers are added, what actually moves in the picture? Two draggable arrows z₁ and z₂ are on stage; the green arrow is their sum z₁ + z₂, drawn by the parallelogram rule (span a parallelogram with z₁, z₂ as adjacent sides and the diagonal is the sum; equivalently, attach z₂’s arrow head-to-tail at z₁’s tip — same landing point). Drag either arrow and the three check rows below verify, row by row, that the sum’s real and imaginary parts are exactly the two sides added separately.

Conclusion: adding z₂ slides the whole picture along z₂’s arrow by exactly that much; the sum’s horizontal and vertical coordinates are the two sides added separately. It is the same thing as vector addition — complex addition = component-wise addition = translation, and it holds for addition only.

Plant a contrast: multiplication is not component-wise. If (1 + i) × (1 + i) were multiplied component-wise you would get something odd like 1 + 1i; the true answer appears on the bench in Step 4 — multiplication moves modulus and angle, not components.

Step 3 · Multiply by i

Multiply by i: Nothing Changes Except a 90° Turn

This step answers: what is i, itself? Pick a starting point and keep pressing “× i”: each press turns the arrow 90° counter-clockwise — watch the readout: the modulus does not budge, the argument gains exactly +90° each time (wrapping back by the principal value past 180°). Landing points and arcs stay on stage the whole time; press four times and the arrow faces its original direction again. Below runs the unit-point tour: 1 → i → −1 → −i → 1, landings pinned one by one on the axes.

Starting point z:
1 (the unit point)
3 + 2i
× i (turn 90°)

Multiplied by i 0 times (every 4 turns restore the direction)

Current z = 1: modulus = 1 (identical before and after ×i); argument = 0°.

The unit-point tour (all computed by repeated multiplication): i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. Watch where i² lands: two 90° turns from 1 are a 180° about-face, landing on −1.

The verdict: ×i = a 90° counter-clockwise rotation, so i² = two turns = an about-face = −1. i² = −1 is turned into existence, not memorised into it. “i is the notation for √−1” and “i is the action of turning 90°” are two faces of the same i: the first is its name, the second is its behaviour.

Switch the start to 3 + 2i and press four more times: the landings are off-axis, yet the modulus stays √13 throughout, the argument gains 90° each press, and the fourth press lands exactly back on (3, 2) — period 4 holds for every start, because four turns are one full turn.

Step 4 · General Multiplication

General Multiplication = Moduli Multiply, Arguments Add: the Checking Bench

This step answers: multiplying by an arbitrary complex number — what happens to modulus and to angle? First verify the two halves separately: multiplying by a positive real (preset 2 below) only scales and never turns; multiplying by a number of modulus 1 only turns and never scales. An arbitrary multiplier z₂ stacks the two. Drag z₁ (the multiplicand) and z₂ (the multiplier); the green arrow is the product z₁·z₂. The bench below checks three groups, all computed live: the modulus check, the angle check, and an algebraic route (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂) — two roads, one source, cross-verified.

All three verdicts come from the same live computation as the main text: landings from repeated multiplication, moduli from Pythagoras — no pre-written answer table. Get one right and it locks (dragging points in the main text afterwards will not wash the verdict away); get one wrong and the feedback diagnoses your exact wrong turn, and you may retry.

Step 6 · Finale

The steady state: the λ = 1 eigenvector, and Google’s starting point

Final stop: a tiny four-node web — A, B, C, D pointing arrows at each other. Imagine a crowd standing on the nodes; at every step each person walks along an outgoing arrow, chosen uniformly at random. That is a Markov chain. Its transition matrix M has, in each column, the probabilities of leaving that column’s node for each row — so every column sums to exactly 1 (nobody vanishes). Start from any distribution and keep multiplying by M: the distribution shifts, then freezes — and a frozen distribution π satisfies Mπ = π: it is an eigenvector of M with eigenvalue exactly λ = 1. Switch the initial distribution and run again: wildly different starts, identical finish. Google’s PageRank treats the whole web as this graph, and the steady distribution is the ranking (real PageRank adds damping: at each step a 0.15 chance of teleporting to a random page, π ← 0.85·Mπ + 0.15/N, to guarantee convergence; this little web is reachable and aperiodic, so it converges undamped).

π ← Mπ, steady state Mπ* = π* — the eigenvector for λ = 1

Initial distribution:
Uniform
All on A
All on D
Random
One step
Play
Run 80 steps
Back to uniform

step k = 0 · distribution (A, B, C, D) = 0.2500, 0.2500, 0.2500, 0.2500 · L1 distance to steady state = 0.3889

Steady state π* = (0.2222, 0.1111, 0.4444, 0.2222) — in theory exactly (2/9, 1/9, 4/9, 2/9): C, pointed to from three places, is the most popular, matching the independent linear-system solve (error < 10⁻¹²). From any start, power iteration returns here.

Column sums of M: 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 (each exactly 1 — total mass is conserved, so an invariant distribution with λ = 1 must exist)

One λ, three faces
PageRank: the steady state is the ranking

Treat pages as nodes and links as arrows, and PageRank is the λ = 1 eigenvector of that giant graph: the page with the largest steady-state share is the most important. It is computed by Step 3’s power iteration — multiply until nothing moves.

Vibration modes: eigenfrequencies

In the vibration equations of bridges and buildings, eigenvectors are the mode shapes (relative sway of each part) and eigenvalues give the natural frequencies. Resonance avoidance and seismic design are, at bottom, eigenvalue problems.

Stability: back to the unit circle

A discrete system x ← Ax is stable ⟺ every eigenvalue satisfies |λ| < 1 — the same sentence as the Z-Transform page’s “poles inside the unit circle”: the system matrix’s eigenvalues ARE the poles. Link: The Z-Transform.

From the circle-squeezing machine to Google’s ranking, there is only one question in between: “which direction refuses to be turned?” Eigenvectors are a matrix’s skeleton — once you see the skeleton, stretching, rotation, vibration, the shape of data and the steady state of a network are all the same story told in different accents.

Step 2 · The Character of λ

All four entries are yours — watch λ change its fate

This step hands you all four entries a, b, c, d. λ₁, λ₂ and the two eigendirection lines are recomputed live, next to two identities: λ₁ + λ₂ must equal the trace tr A = a + d, and λ₁λ₂ must equal the determinant — the residuals hover around 10⁻¹⁵, floating point’s last stand. Tour the presets: a negative eigenvalue flips its arrow; both λ below 1 shrink the whole circle; the shear has only one eigendirection (a repeated, defective root — the page honestly draws just one line); the rotation–scaling has discriminant below zero, so real eigendirections do not exist — λ is a complex-conjugate pair, and the page will not fake a direction for you; it shows the true behavior instead: a spiral.

λ = (tr A ± √( (a−d)² + 4bc )) / 2, discriminant Δ = (a−d)² + 4bc

λ₁ = 2.4485
λ₂ = 0.7515
λ₁+λ₂ = 3.2000 · tr A = 3.2000 · residual 0
λ₁λ₂ = 1.8400 · det A = 1.8400 · residual 0
discriminant Δ = 2.880

a (top-left) 2.20
b (top-right) 0.60
c (bottom-left) 0.60

Back to default [[2.2,0.6],[0.6,1.0]]

How to read a negative λ: λ = −1 does not mean “shrunk by −1×”; it means flip the direction, then scale by |λ|. You already dragged one in Step 1’s third preset. Complex λ is not broken math either: it honestly reports a rotation hiding inside the transformation — bridges, AC circuits and quantum mechanics are full of complex eigenvalues.

← 知识索引

复数 · 乘法是旋转加伸缩

课本里 i 是空降的：「规定 i² = −1」，背下来、会算、但不知道它是什么。这一页换个讲法：先把数从一条线请回一张平面——复数（形如 a + bi 的数，a、b 都是实数）就是平面上的一个点、一根箭头；加法是把箭头平移，乘法是把箭头旋转加伸缩。于是 i² = −1 不必背：乘 i 就是转 90°，转两次正好掉头指向 −1。这一页所有的模、辐角、和、积，都只由 (a, b) 当场实算，图和读数同源。

中
EN
0 数轴不够用
1 点与箭头
2 加法是平移
3 乘 i 转 90°
4 乘法对账台
5 自测
6 终章

第 0 步 · 数轴不够用

数轴不够用：x² = −1 的解站在哪里？

这一步要回答：方程 x² = −1 的解，到底站在哪里？你已经知道：实数全排在一条数轴上，而任何实数的平方都 ≥ 0——正数平方是正数，负数平方也是正数，0 的平方是 0。下面这台探针让你亲手验：拖着 x 沿数轴走，上方描出的轨迹是 x² 的全部取值，它贴着数轴上方走，却永远够不到 −1 那条横线。找不到不是因为没找仔细——是这条线上根本没有它的位置。

平方探针 x（沿数轴拖） x = 1
把数轴竖起来当一条边：展开平面 ⤢

探针 x = 1：x² = 1 ≥ 0。把 x 从负拖到正，平方一路描出一条抛物线，最低点就是 0——离 −1 还差着整整一条「够不到」的距离。

结论：x² = −1 在实数里无解，缺的不是某个数、是一个维度。给数轴加一条垂直的轴，数就从「线上的点」升级为「平面上的点」；新轴上的单位记作 i。这一步先只承诺一件事：i² = −1 在本页会变成看得见的事实，不靠背。

为什么非得加一整条轴，而不是只添一个点？因为数要能运算：添进来的点和原来的实数相加、相乘，结果还得有地方站——一张平面才装得下这一整套新数。下一站先把「平面上的点」这套读法认全。

开始探索 ↓

第 1 步 · 复平面上的点

复数是平面上的点：钉住它要么 (a, b)，要么（模，辐角）

这一步要回答：一个复数，要几个数才能钉住？图上是一个复平面：横轴是实轴、纵轴是虚轴。拖动点 z，读数四栏全部由它的坐标 (a, b) 当场实算：a 叫实部、b 叫虚部（注意：虚部是 b 这个实数本身，不带 i），写法记作 z = a + bi；从原点向 z 拉出的箭头，长度叫模 |z|——就是勾股定理里那根斜边；箭头与实轴正半轴的夹角（逆时针量）叫辐角 θ。辐角有很多个等价写法，本页统一取辐角主值：归到 (−180°, 180°] 里的那一个。

坐标输入 · 键盘或数值

绘图范围：实部、虚部分别限制到 −5…5。这是图的范围，不是复数的数学范围。

3 + 4i

z ≈ 3 + 4i：实部 a ≈ 3，虚部 b ≈ 4；模 |z| = √(a² + b²) ≈ 5（斜边由勾股实算）；辐角 θ ≈ 53.1°（从实轴正半轴逆时针量）。数字由未舍入坐标计算后显示为近似值。

结论：钉住一个点有两套办法——坐标 (a, b)，或者（模，辐角）。它们是同一根箭头的两种读法：前者说「向右走几、向上走几」，后者说「多长、朝哪个方向」。下一步加法用第一套读法最顺，乘法则要靠第二套——先都认熟。

边界逐个验：把点拖到负实轴上，辐角读作 +180° 而不是 −180°——主值区间的右端是闭的。拖到单位圆上（虚线圈）时模恒为 1，只剩角度在变；这时箭头尖的坐标正是 (cos θ, sin θ)，这个读法的出处在三角函数页第 1 步。

第 2 步 · 加法

加法 = 平移：和的坐标就是两边坐标各自相加

这一步要回答：两个复数相加，图上到底动了什么？图上有两根可拖的箭头 z₁、z₂，第三根绿箭头是它们的和 z₁ + z₂，用平行四边形法则画出（以 z₁、z₂ 为邻边张成平行四边形，对角线就是和；等价地看，z₂ 的箭头首尾相接到 z₁ 的尖端，落点相同）。拖任意一根，下面三栏对账会逐栏核对：和的实部、虚部是不是恰好两边各自相加。

输入有限坐标；Tab 切换控件，↑/↓ 只把当前草稿增减 0.1，Enter 或应用才更新图。与拖动相同：先吸附到 0.1 网格，再按下面的绘图范围限制。下方读数给出实际应用值。

绘图范围：每个输入复数的两分量分别限制到 −4.2…4.2；和仍由两数实算。此范围只为绘图。

z₂ · 第二个数

z₁ = 2 + i，z₂ = 1 + 2i，z₁ + z₂ = 3 + 3i

实部对账：2 + 1 = 3 ✓（正是和的实部）

虚部对账：1 + 2 = 3 ✓（正是和的虚部）

结论：加 z₂，就是把整幅图沿 z₂ 这根箭头平移那么远；和的横、纵坐标恰是两边各自相加。这与向量加法是同一件事——复数加法 = 分量相加 = 平移，只对加法成立。

先埋一个反差：乘法不是分量相乘。(1 + i) × (1 + i) 若按分量乘会得 1 + 1i 之类怪东西，真实答案第 4 步在对账台上见——乘法动的是模和角，不是分量。

第 3 步 · 乘 i

乘 i：什么都不改，只转 90°

这一步要回答：i 自己到底「是」什么？选一个起点，按「× i」按钮连着按：每按一次，箭头就逆时针转 90°——盯住读数：模纹丝不动，辐角每次恰好 +90°（超过 180° 就按主值归回来）。落点和弧线全程留痕，连按四次，箭头回到原来的方向。下面还有一条单位点巡演：1 → i → −1 → −i → 1，落点逐个钉在坐标轴上。

起点 z：
1（单位点）
3 + 2i
× i（转 90°）
重置 ↺
已乘 i 0 次（每 4 次回到原方向）

当前 z = 1：模 = 1（乘 i 前后一模一样）；辐角 = 0°。

单位点巡演（全部由连乘实算）：i¹ = i，i² = −1，i³ = −i，i⁴ = 1。看 i² 落在哪：从 1 出发转两次 90° 就是掉头 180°，落在 −1 上。

收口：×i = 逆时针旋转 90°，所以 i² = 转两次 = 掉头 = −1。i² = −1 是转出来的，不是背出来的。「i 是 √−1 的记号」和「i 是转 90° 的动作」是同一个 i 的两副面孔：前者是它的名字，后者是它的行为。

换起点 3 + 2i 再连按四次：四个落点不在坐标轴上，但模始终是 √13、辐角每次 +90°、第四次严丝合缝回到 (3, 2)——周期 4 对任何起点都成立，因为转四次就是转一整圈。

第 4 步 · 一般乘法

一般乘法 = 模相乘、角相加：对账台

这一步要回答：乘上任意一个复数，模和角各发生什么？先把两件事分开验明：乘一个正实数（如下方预设 2）只伸缩不转；乘一个模为 1 的数只转不伸缩。任意乘数 z₂ 则是两件事叠加。拖动 z₁（被乘）与 z₂（乘数），绿箭头是乘积 z₁·z₂；下面对账台三组读数全部实算：模对账、角对账、还有一条代数路 (a₁a₂ − b₁b₂, a₁b₂ + b₁a₂)——两条路同源互证。

本演台把两个点限制在模 ≤ 2.6 的圆盘内，免得乘积跑出图外——法则本身对任意大小的复数都成立。先用预设 1 + i 验一组：z₁ = 2 + i 时乘积辐角应比原来恰好多 45°、模恰好多乘 √2，对账台会当场打勾。

第 5 步 · 自测

自测：转得对不对，当场验

三道题的判定都由与正文同源的实算给出：落点由连乘算、模由勾股算，不预设答案表。答对一题锁定一题（答题后去拖正文的点，不会冲掉这里的判定）；答错会按你的错法给出诊断，可以再试。

z = 3 + 2i，连乘两次 i（即 z·i²），落在哪里？先在心里转：一次 90°、再一次 90°。

第 6 步 · 终章

终章：一张平面，两种运算

复数不是一条要背的法则，是把数放回平面之后自然长出来的运算。收口三张卡：

复数是平面上的点

z = a + bi 与平面上的点、与从原点出发的箭头一一对应。钉住它有两种读法：坐标 (a, b)，或（模，辐角）——模是箭头的长度，辐角是它的方向（本页取主值 (−180°, 180°]）。

加法是平移

和的坐标 = 两边坐标各自相加，图上就是沿着加数的箭头平移一次——平行四边形的对角线。加法只动位置，不动方向和长度的读法。

乘法是旋转 + 伸缩

模相乘、角相加：乘上谁，就按谁的模伸缩、按谁的辐角旋转。乘 i 是其中最纯粹的一例——模 1、角 90°，只转不伸缩；i² = −1 就是「转两次正好掉头」。

两个方向先各留一句话：除法是乘法的逆——角相减、模相除，本页不展开。再往前一步埋一条线：如果这个点自己转起来、角度随时间均匀长大，它的位置就是 eiθ 在单位圆上跑——那是欧拉公式的入口，本页只点名。
